desc:
Cut the string s into consecutive non-empty pieces so that every piece is a palindrome. Return all possible ways to do this.

Describe one way by the lengths of its pieces from left to right (the lengths add up to s.length). For "aab" the answer is [[1, 1, 1], [2, 1]], meaning a|a|b and aa|b. Different ways are different rows, and no way appears twice. The rows may be returned in any order.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Decide the first piece, then solve the same problem for the rest of the string. Which first pieces are allowed?

Recurse on a start index i. For every end index j ≥ i such that s[i..j] is a palindrome, record the length j - i + 1, recurse from j + 1, then undo the choice. When i reaches n, store a copy of the lengths.
Do not re-test palindromes from scratch every time: precompute pal[i][j] with pal[i][j] = (s[i] == s[j]) and pal[i+1][j-1] (a length 1 or 2 range needs only the first part).
editorial: This is the standard "choose the next piece" backtracking. The state is the index i where the next piece starts and the list of piece lengths chosen so far. For each j from i to n - 1, if s[i..j] is a palindrome, push j - i + 1, recurse on j + 1 and pop. Reaching i == n means the whole string has been consumed, so a copy of the current list is one complete answer.

A palindrome table filled in O(n2) removes the repeated palindrome checks. The cost is then proportional to the output: a string such as aaaa...a has 2n-1 partitions (every cut can be chosen or not), so the worst case is O(n · 2n) time for writing the answers.
Since a partition is completely described by its cut positions, using piece lengths as the encoding makes rows unique and easy to compare.
space: O(n<sup>2</sup>) for the table plus the output
